title: People are health
hook: a 2010 review linked strong social ties to longer life (Holt-Lunstad et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday: as to a friend. When you slipped up, did you ask what you'd say to a friend, and say it? Today, the friends themselves. Day three hundred fifteen.

Think of the health advice you hear most. Stop smoking. Move more. Eat your vegetables. Sleep. Now think of the advice you almost never hear from a doctor: call your sister. Have dinner with your neighbors. Keep the friend who makes you laugh. It sounds like greeting-card stuff, the soft extra you get to once the real health work is done. In 2010 a team of researchers gathered up nearly a hundred and fifty studies, following hundreds of thousands of people for years, and asked a hard question: do the people with stronger relationships actually live longer? Today, to close our week: people are health.
screen: `STOP SMOKING. MOVE MORE. SLEEP.` → `CALL YOUR SISTER?` → `A HARD QUESTION, ASKED CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: First, the finding. Julianne Holt-Lunstad and her colleagues combined 148 studies with more than three hundred thousand people, followed on average for about seven and a half years. People with stronger social relationships were about fifty percent more likely to be alive at the end of the studies than people with weaker ones. The authors noted that the size of that link was comparable to well-known risks like smoking. Second, remember compared to what. These were mostly observational studies. Healthy people may find it easier to keep friends, and many things travel together. The researchers tried to adjust for age, health and other factors, and the link held, but a review like this shows a strong association, not proof that a phone call adds a year. Still, the size of it made many public-health researchers take loneliness seriously. Third, the old voices, each in its own house. Ecclesiastes in the Hebrew Bible says two are better than one, because if one falls, the other can lift him up. The Stoic Seneca wrote letters to his friend Lucilius about how rare and how needed a true friend is. And Kahlil Gibran, in The Prophet, put it in one line: "Your friend is your needs answered." Fourth, the week behind us, which this caps. The talking mind. Sixty-six days. After the kettle. Easy beats heroic. Compassion can grow. As to a friend. And now, other people. Every habit we built this week gets easier with company, and kinder. It turns out company isn't the reward after the health work. It's part of the work.
screen: `148 STUDIES, 300,000 PEOPLE.` · `STRONG LINK, NOT PROOF.` · `TWO ARE BETTER THAN ONE.` · `YOUR FRIEND IS YOUR NEEDS ANSWERED.` · then, large: `PEOPLE ARE HEALTH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you haven't talked to in a while. A friend who drifted. A cousin. An old neighbor. Let their faces pass by, one at a time, without guilt. Then pick one. Picture them answering the phone. Picture their voice. Decide when today you'll call or message them, even just two lines. Then rest with that face in mind. The bell holds the time.
People are health. Strong social ties are linked to a longer life, about as strongly as some of the best-known health risks. Today's word.
Your line: people are health. Call the person you chose today. Not a like, not a heart: a voice, or at least a real message. Day three hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Public-health researchers now treat social connection as a health factor, and many traditions build practice around community, from shared meals to weekly gatherings; people on their own paths often keep a regular call or meal with friends.
